q: The store's phone number is saved on every one of its 10,000 order rows. The phone changes, and a script updates only 9,000 of them. What is this problem called?
options: The update problem: a fact saved many times will one day disagree with itself
The insert problem
A phantom read
A deadlock
why: One fact, one place. If you copy it, you must decide who keeps the copy right.

q: A single table holds orders with the store details inside. What goes wrong when you delete a store's last order?
options: Nothing, the store stays in the table
The store itself disappears from the data
Postgres blocks the delete
The next order gets the same id
why: A table with the store inside the order cannot hold a store with no orders. Deleting the last order deletes the store.

q: Which of these breaks 1NF (first normal form)?
options: A column that holds a number
A table that has a primary key
A column that holds a list, like 'red,blue,green'
Two tables that point to each other
why: 1NF means no lists. 2NF means no half of a key. 3NF means no facts about another column.

q: Why save the price paid on the order line, instead of reading the product's current price?
options: It makes the order table smaller
Postgres cannot join the product table
It is required by third normal form
A price paid is a fact about a moment. The product price can change later, but the order must not
why: This is a copy on purpose. Save it on the order line and never update it.

q: A report query is slow. What should you try BEFORE you save a copy of the data?
options: Add an index, and measure the slow read. Copy only if it is still too slow
Copy the data right away, because copies are always faster
Move the table to another database
Turn off foreign keys
why: Every copy needs an owner and a check that compares the copy with the truth. So try an index first.
